newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony quarterly profits double; outlook strong.
newsitem.headline: Sony quarterly profits double; outlook strong.

text.p: Electronics giant Sony Corp. said Wednesday its profits more than doubled in the latest quarter and predicted earnings would climb to a record high for the year, powered by strong sales of electronic goods and a weak yen.

"Almost all of our electronic products -- especially videogame players, minidiscs and camcoders -- are doing well ... in all markets," Sony's financial director Sumio Sano told a news conference. "The entertainment and insurance businesses are also making equally large contributions to our group profit," he said.
The strong quarterly performance led Sony to revise its group sales and profit forecasts sharply upward for the year to the end of March.

Sony now expects group net profit of 132 billion yen ($1.07 billion), nearly 2.5 times the net profit in the 1995/96 business year, on sales of 5.5 trillion yen ($44.7 billion), up 20 percent, both record highs.
For the October-December quarter, Sony reported group net profit of 75.38 billion yen ($612 million), up 103 percent, and sales of 1.67 trillion yen ($13.5 billion), up 23.4 percent.
Analysts had largely expected upward revisions but they said the revised figures were larger than their estimates.
Their forecasts for the firm's yearly group net profit ranged from 122 billion yen ($991 million) to 130 billion yen ($1.05 billion).
"Sony is now the company with the lowest risk and the highest return," said Hitoshi Kuriyama, an analyst at Goldman Sachs (Japan) Corp.

"Helped by a strategy to create new markets with innovative products and a strong brand image, Sony tends to stay away from cut-throat price competition, which is now hurting rivals such as Matsushita Electric and Pioneer," he said.

Sony's Sano said sales increased for all major electronic products, including TVs, videocassette recorders and CD players, in October-December, except for the Walkman, which suffered growing competition from products in its own camp -- minidiscs.
"It is very hard to pick out only one product that buoyed our earnings," Sano said.
Analysts said the 32-bit PlayStation gameplayer would be one of the biggest factors in boosting profits.
Sony sold 11 million PlayStations on the global market since its launch in December 1994, overwhelming rivals Nintendo Co. Ltd and Sega Enterprises Ltd.
Sano said sales in the picture entertainment division jumped 35 percent in dollar terms in the quarter as bigger sales of TV programmes offset continued doldrums in film-making.
Analysts say among the few concerns in Sony's business is the computer peripherals unit, such as CD-ROMs and chips, where prices are declining sharply, particularly in the United States.
But Kazuya Yamamoto, an analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research, expects the division to become profitable in the second half of the current business year.
Any sharp recovery of the yen would also dent Sony as 65 percent of its sales comes from exports. Sano said, however, that Sony does not expect a sharp recovery of the yen to start soon.
"If global economies remain steady and there is no sharp yen recovery Sony will be able to report a more than 10 percent increase in group sales in the year starting April 1," he said.
